subject: CTDS Snapshots - effective t with inconsistent camera performance

messages.author: ebccda9c6e843a4e
messages.subject: CTDS Snapshots - effective t with inconsistent camera performance
parts:
Hi all,

I think this builds on a previous conversation on here from a couple of years ago about the definition of snapshot moments and less-than-perfect camera trap functionality (https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/5InaOLHIMHs/m/j8r2g-ezAQAJ).

I am looking into using effective t values based on camera trapping rate and recovery times. However, one of the camera models used in my study has been maddeningly inconsistent with burst times.  See data below for a 5 image burst:

I understand effective t values derived from camera trapping rates have previously been calculated using a mean burst time across all cameras used in the study. But, as you can see, the average burst time varies significantly between individual cameras in my study, which is making defining a single snapshot based on the camera functionality tricky.

As I am using two different camera models, I am already calculating effort based on the respective cameras Effective Detection Area, but with this inconsistency, particularly with camera 10, I'm wondering if there is any statistical limitation to calculate t, and subsequently effort, on a site-specific basis (as shown in the table)?

Thanks, 

Victoria

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] CTDS Snapshots - effective t with inconsistent camera performance
parts:
Victoria

Thanks for your question. I don't think we have any experience/research that directly addresses this question, so I can't provide a definitive answer. But my opinion is that calculating the number of snapshot moments for each camera, based upon the camera-specific t (as you show in your table), is probably fine.

The utility of this email list is that you can potentially get other opinions from folks more intimately acquainted with camera trap analyses.
